                                     PROJECT NO. 58481

 RULEMAKING TO IMPLEMENT                         §        PUBLIC UTILITY COMMISSION
 LARGE LOAD INTERCONNECTION                      §
 STANDARDS UNDER PURA 37.0561                    §                  OF TEXAS


                   COMMENTS OF BLACK MOUNTAINPOWER, LLC

                                     I.​   INTRODUCTION

       Black Mountain Power, LLC (“Black Mountain”) is a private, entrepreneurial energy,

power, and natural resources company with extensive experience in sourcing, developing, and

operating projects across these thematics in both the United States and Australia. Black

Mountain has transacted on more than $2 billion of projects over 18 years, and one of Black

Mountain’s business units has originated as lead developer over 3.5 GW of energy storage

projects across Texas. We are currently developing more than 15 data center projects across the

ERCOT region.

       As noted at the January 9th workshop, Black Mountain understands the need to

differentiate between viable and speculative loads requesting interconnection in ERCOT, but

emphasizes that this process be executed in a way that does not bar credible large load

developers with a history of successful investments in Texas from development by setting

unnecessarily high costs. We appreciate the opportunity to provide follow-up comments on this

rulemaking in response to the workshop and look forward to working collaboratively with

commission staff to develop refined, mutually agreeable language to this rule.
                           II.​   DISCUSSION DRAFT FEEDBACK

Financial Security:

       The most concerning aspect of the proposed language continues to be the $50,000/MW

security requirement as suggested in §25.194(e)(8) of the staff’s discussion draft. The proposed

collateral requirement is excessive and risks undermining the purpose of ensuring that only

well-capitalized projects populate the queue. Looking at the responses to the previous round of

comments from stakeholders, the proposed $/MW security from each stakeholder is as follows:
         As demonstrated in the numbers, the average proposed security amount is ~$28,000, and

the median proposed amount was $20,000. It’s important for commission staff to recognize that

there are outliers on both ends of these proposed dollar amounts, but the correct value likely lies

somewhere in the middle. When this data was presented at the workshop, there appeared to be

broad agreement that a $/MW value closer to $20,000 was more reasonable. The representative

for Oncor spoke up in agreement at the workshop, stating that the $100,000 value is “excessive

in [Oncor’s] perspective.”1

        Holding the money would also be placing an “administrative burden” on the utility to

maintain the capital. AEP noted that “As utilities, we’re really good at being utilities. We’re not

really set up to be great banks.”2 This reality reinforces the importance of setting the security at

the lowest level consistent with policy goals, since utilities have been clear that maintaining large

collateral accounts would impose unnecessary administrative strain.

        Finally, as previously stated, our organization is currently advancing more than 15 data

center projects across ERCOT. Under the proposed framework, we would be required to post

over $750 million in collateral which would translate into $80–100 million annually in interest

and carrying costs, an untenable burden with no guarantee of process, timing, or outcome. The

representative from Oncor agreed at the workshop that this is unnecessarily burdensome, stating

that the $/MW security should not “set the standards so high that it breaks [developers] backs by

requiring them to post a security that no one can handle.”3 Such requirements would inevitably

lead to widespread cancellations, as no developer can justify immobilizing this scale of funding

absent certainty in study results or repayment timelines.

        SB6 must balance the dual goals of encouraging broad economic development and

ensuring the seriousness of load filings. Black Mountain has transacted on more than $2 billion

of projects over 18 years and our Energy Storage team has originated 3.5 GW of energy storage

projects across Texas, directly contributing to grid resiliency and reliability. Yet even with this

level of sophistication and demonstrated commitment, the proposed deposit fees would

effectively preclude our ability to develop data center projects in Texas.

In-Flight Projects:

       The proposed language does not clearly address how new requirements would apply to

projects that have already initiated load interconnection studies, commonly referred to as

“in‑flight” projects. Black Mountain currently has multiple projects in this category and has

already committed substantial capital to interconnecting utilities to begin large‑load

interconnection assessments. At present, it remains unclear whether the CIAC requirement will

apply retroactively or whether a $/MW security will be imposed on these projects.

       It is essential that the Commission establish clear rules governing the treatment of

in‑flight projects. Specifically, the Commission should provide a definitive cut‑off date or filing

milestone to determine which projects are subject to the new requirements. These projects should

also not be subject to further delays and unnecessarily restudied multiple times.

       Black Mountain additionally believes that filing sequence, meaning the timeline in which

projects submitted their interconnection requests, must be considered to avoid

disenfranchisement. Projects that filed earlier and have advanced further in the study process

should not be disadvantaged relative to later entrants. These projects have already faced

significant delays and should not be subject to even further delays due to an out-of-sequence

assessment of loads seeking interconnection. Recognizing filing sequence as a factor would
 ensure fairness, protect prior investments, and maintain confidence in the integrity of the

interconnection process.

       Black Mountain believes quarterly batches of qualified projects with similar filing

chronology is appropriate. Quarterly batching is the most practical approach because overly

large, less frequent batches risk spreading available capacity too thinly across too many projects.

For instance, if a semi-annual batch were to include 100 projects and the utility were to release 3

GWs of capacity, the resulting 30 MW average would likely be insufficient for many projects to

achieve liftoff. Quarterly batching allows for smaller cohorts that are more likely to ensure that

each project will receive a sufficient capacity allocation to reach a viable operating size.
                                  III.​   CONCLUSION

We greatly appreciate the Commission staff’s work on this issue and consideration of our

perspective.

                                               Respectfully submitted,

​                                              /s/ Rhett Bennett
​                                              Rhett Bennett
​                                              Chief Executive Officer
​                                              Black Mountain Power, LLC

                                   PROJECT NO. 58481

RULEMAKING TO IMPLEMENT                       §         PUBLIC UTILITY COMMISSION
LARGE LOAD INTERCONNECTION                    §
STANDARDS UNDER PURA 37.0561                  §                    OF TEXAS


         EXECUTIVE SUMMARY OF BLACK MOUNTAIN POWER, LLC

 ●​ Black Mountain believes the proposed $50,000/MW collateral requirement is excessive,

    creates prohibitive burdens, and risks deterring serious developers. Black Mountain

    proposes a more reasonable ceiling of $10,000/MW.

 ●​ Excessive collateral requirements will drive away capable developers. A balanced

    approach is needed to preserve queue integrity while sustaining investment.

 ●​ Black Mountain stresses that the current language fails to clarify how requirements apply

    to “in‑flight” projects already undergoing studies. Clear guidance is essential for fairness.

 ●​ Black Mountain encourages Commission staff to balance economic burden with the

    seriousness of load filings. Overemphasis on collateral risks eliminating viable projects

    and undermining Texas’s ability to attract investment and strengthen resiliency.

 ●​ Black Mountain believes quarterly batches of qualified projects with similar filing

    chronology is appropriate to ensure cohorts small enough that allow each project to

    receive a sufficient MW allocation to develop.

 ●​ Black Mountain has demonstrated through years of successful development that we have

    a track record of successful execution. We are an example of how excessive requirements

    for collateral would increase costs of successful developers, exceedingly impair market

    access and participation, and ultimately lead to less successful data center developments

    in Texas.
